title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 121 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 592–594 (Night 121, continuing directly from nights-120), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 121 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. The lady grieves for his dead cousin ʿAzīza, who kept her own love secret and yet helped him to reach her, and asks to be taken to the grave. There she gives away a purse of dinars in ʿAzīza’s name and cuts a poem into the headstone. For a year ʿAzīz lives with her in ease and forgets his cousin; then one evening, perfumed and drunk, he wanders into a lane where an old woman comes towards him with a lighted candle and a rolled-up letter. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-first night,

sentences.t: قٰلَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الشَّابَّ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ قَالَتْ لِي إِنِّي أَخَافُ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَقَعَ فِي رَزِيَّةٍ فَمَا تَلْقَى مَنْ يُخَلِّصُكَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba qāla li-tāji al-mulūki thumma inna al-ṣabiyyata qālat lī innī akhāfu ʿalayka an taqaʿa fī raziyyatin fa-mā talqā man yukhalliṣuka minhā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth said to Tāj al-Mulūk: Then the girl said to me: I fear for you that you fall into a calamity, and you (will) not find who (will) deliver you from it.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man said to Tāj al-Mulūk: Then the young woman said to me, “I fear you will fall into some calamity, and find no one to get you out of it.
sentences.n: The night opens by going back over the last words of the night before. The print spells qālat, “she said”, as قلت, without its long ā, a defective spelling the edition often uses; it is pointed here with a dagger alif. The print puts a shadda on رزيّة (raziyya, “calamity”).

sentences.t: فَوَاحَسْرَتَاهْ عَلَى بِنْتِ عَمِّكَ وَلَيْتَنِي عَلِمْتُ بِهَا قَبْلَ مَوْتِهَا حَتَّى كُنْتُ أُكَافِئُهَا عَلَى مَا فَعَلَتْ مَعِي مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَأَزُورُهَا رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-wā-ḥasratāh ʿalā binti ʿammika wa-laytanī ʿalimtu bihā qabla mawtihā ḥattā kuntu ukāfiʾuhā ʿalā mā faʿalat maʿī mina al-maʿrūfi wa-azūruhā raḥmatu allāhi taʿālā ʿalayhā
sentences.l: So alas, O my grief, over the daughter of your uncle! And would that I had known of her before her death, so that I might have repaid her for what she did with me of the kindness, and visited her — the mercy of God, exalted (is) He, (be) upon her!
sentences.i: Alas, how I grieve for your cousin! Would that I had known of her before she died, so that I could have repaid her for the kindness she did me, and visited her — God’s mercy be on her!
sentences.n: wā-ḥasratāh, “O my grief!”: wā- is the particle of lament, and the ending -āh draws the cry out. ʿalima bi-, “know of, learn about”: the verb chooses the bi-. ḥattā kuntu ukāfiʾuhā, “so that I would have repaid her”: kuntu with an imperfect, for what would have followed.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهَا كَتَمَتْ سِرَّهَا وَلَمْ تَبُحْ بِمَا عِنْدَهَا وَلَوْلَاهَا مَا كُنْتَ وَصَلْتَ إِلَيَّ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-innahā katamat sirrahā wa-lam tabuḥ bi-mā ʿindahā wa-lawlāhā mā kunta waṣalta ilayya abadan
sentences.l: For she kept-hidden her secret and did not disclose what (was) with her; and were it not for her, you would not have reached to me, ever.
sentences.i: For she kept her secret and never told what was in her heart; and but for her you would never have reached me.
sentences.n: bāḥa bi-, “disclose, let out”: the verb chooses the bi-. lawlāhā, “were it not for her”: lawlā takes the pronoun directly. The print itself marks kunta, “you were”, and the shadda of ilayya, “to me”.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي أَشْتَهِي عَلَيْكَ أَمْرًا فَقُلْتُ مَا هُوَ قَالَتْ وَهُوَ أَنْ تُوصِلَنِي إِلَى قَبْرِهَا حَتَّى أَزُورَهَا فِى الْقَبْرِ الَّذِي هِيَ فِيهِ وَأَكْتُبَ عَلَيْهِ أَبْيَاتًا
sentences.tr: wa-innī ashtahī ʿalayka amran fa-qultu mā huwa qālat wa-huwa an tūṣilanī ilā qabrihā ḥattā azūrahā fī al-qabri alladhī hiya fīhi wa-aktuba ʿalayhi abyātan
sentences.l: And I desire upon you a thing. And I said: What (is) it? She said: And it (is) that you bring me to her grave, so that I visit her in the grave which she (is) in it, and write upon it verses.
sentences.i: And there is something I would ask of you.” I said, “What is it?” She said, “That you take me to her grave, so that I may visit her in the grave where she lies and write some verses on it.”
sentences.n: ishtahā ʿalā, “wish (something) of someone”: a spoken way of asking a favour. alladhī hiya fīhi, “which she is in it”: Arabic takes up the relative with a pronoun, here fīhi.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا فِي غَدٍ إِنْ شَاءَاللَّهُ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā fī ghadin in shāʾa allāhu taʿālā
sentences.l: And I said to her: In tomorrow, if God, exalted (is) He, wills.
sentences.i: I said to her, “Tomorrow, if God Most High wills.”
sentences.n: The print runs شاء and الله together.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي نِمْتُ مَعَهَا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَهِيَ بَعْدَ كُلِّ سَاعَةٍ تَقُولُ لِي لَيْتَكَ أَخْبَرْتَنِي بِبِنْتِ عَمِّكَ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innī nimtu maʿahā tilka al-laylata wa-hiya baʿda kulli sāʿatin taqūlu lī laytaka akhbartanī bi-binti ʿammika qabla mawtihā
sentences.l: Then I slept with her that the night, and she, after every hour, says to me: Would that you had informed me of the daughter of your uncle before her death!
sentences.i: Then I slept with her that night, and every little while she would say to me, “If only you had told me about your cousin before she died!”
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “inform of, tell about”: the verb chooses the bi-, which here sits on bint, “daughter”. baʿda kulli sāʿatin, “after every hour”: every so often.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَامَعْنَي هٰذَيْنِ الْكَلِمَتَيْنِ اللَّتَيْنِ قَالَتْهُمَا وَهُمَا الْوَفَاءُ مَلِيحٌ * وَالْغَدْرُ قَبِيحٌ * فَلَمْ تُجِبْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā mā maʿnā hādhayni al-kalimatayni allatayni qālathumā wa-humā al-wafāʾu malīḥun * wa-al-ghadru qabīḥun * fa-lam tujibnī
sentences.l: And I said to her: What (is the) meaning of these two words which she said, and they (are): Faithfulness (is) fine; * and treachery (is) foul? * And she did not answer me.
sentences.i: I asked her, “What do they mean, those two sayings she spoke: ‘Faithfulness is fair, and treachery is foul’?” But she gave me no answer.
sentences.n: The print runs ما and معنى together and spells maʿnā, “meaning”, with a dotted yāʾ (معني). hādhayni al-kalimatayni: the masculine “these two” with the feminine kalima, as in the night before; the relative allatayni after it is feminine.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَ الصَّبَاحُ قَامَتْ وَأَخَذَتْ كِيسًا فِيهِ دَنَانِيرُ وَقَالَتْ لِي قُمْ وَأَرِنِي قَبْرَهَا حَتَّى أَزُورَهُ وَأَكْتُبَ عَلَيْهِ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ وَأَعْمَلَ عَلَيْهِ قُبَّةً وَأَتَرَحَّمَ عَلَيْهَا وَأَصْرِفَ هٰذِهِ الدَّنَانِيرَ صَدَقَةً عَنْ رُوحِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kāna al-ṣabāḥu qāmat wa-akhadhat kīsan fīhi danānīru wa-qālat lī qum wa-arinī qabrahā ḥattā azūrahu wa-aktuba ʿalayhi hādhihi al-abyāta wa-aʿmala ʿalayhi qubbatan wa-ataraḥḥama ʿalayhā wa-aṣrifa hādhihi al-danānīra ṣadaqatan ʿan rūḥihā
sentences.l: And when it was the morning, she rose and took a purse, in it (were) dinars, and said to me: Rise and show me her grave, so that I visit it and write upon it these the verses, and make over it a dome, and ask-mercy upon her, and spend these the dinars (as) alms on behalf of her soul.
sentences.i: When morning came she rose, took a purse with dinars in it, and said to me, “Get up and show me her grave, so that I may visit it, write these verses on it, raise a dome over it, pray for God’s mercy on her, and spend these dinars in alms for her soul.”
sentences.n: qubba, “dome”: a small domed shrine raised over a grave; the print puts a shadda on it. taraḥḥama ʿalā, “ask God’s mercy for”. ṣadaqatan ʿan rūḥihā, “alms on behalf of her soul”: charity given in the dead woman’s name, its merit counted to her.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً ثُمَّ مَشَيْتُ قُدَّامَهَا وَمَشَتْ خَلْفِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan thumma mashaytu quddāmahā wa-mashat khalfī
sentences.l: And I said to her: Hearing and obedience. Then I walked in front of her, and she walked behind me.
sentences.i: I answered her with hearing and obedience; then I walked ahead of her, and she followed behind me.
sentences.n: samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “(I give) hearing and obedience”: the stock words of consent. The print puts a shadda on quddām, “in front of”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَتْ تَتَصَدَّقُ وَهِيَ مَاشِيَةٌ فِى الطَّرِيقِ وَكُلَّمَا تَصَدَّقَتْ صَدَقَةً تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الصَّدَقَةُ عَنْ رُوحِ عَزِيزَةَ الَّتِي كَتَمَتْ سِرَّهَا حَتَّي شَرِبَتْ كَاسَ مَنُونِهَا وَلَابَاحَتْ بِسِرِّ هَوَاهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārat tataṣaddaqu wa-hiya māshiyatun fī al-ṭarīqi wa-kullamā taṣaddaqat ṣadaqatan taqūlu hādhihi al-ṣadaqatu ʿan rūḥi ʿAzīzata allatī katamat sirrahā ḥattā sharibat kāsa manūnihā wa-lā bāḥat bi-sirri hawāhā
sentences.l: And she began giving-alms while she (was) walking on the road; and whenever she gave an alms she says: This the alms (is) on behalf of the soul of ʿAzīza, who kept-hidden her secret until she drank the cup of her death, and did not disclose the secret of her love.
sentences.i: As she walked along the road she gave alms, and each time she gave she said, “This alms is for the soul of ʿAzīza, who kept her secret until she drank the cup of her death, and never betrayed the secret of her love.”
sentences.n: ṣārat tataṣaddaqu, “she took to giving alms”: ṣāra with an imperfect, “begin to do”. manūn, “death, fate”: a word of poetry; the cup of death is an old figure. wa-lā bāḥat, “and did not disclose”: lā with a perfect, a literary “and not”; bāḥa bi- chooses the bi-. The print spells kaʾs, “cup”, without its hamza (كاس; read kās, as spoken) and ḥattā with a dotted yāʾ (حتي), and runs ولا and باحت together.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَتَصَدَّقُ مِنَ الْكِيسِ وَتَقُولُ عَنْ رُوحِ عَزِيزَةَ حَتَّى نَفِدَ مَا فِى الْكِيسِ وَوَصَلْنَا إِلَى الْقَبْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal tataṣaddaqu mina al-kīsi wa-taqūlu ʿan rūḥi ʿAzīzata ḥattā nafida mā fī al-kīsi wa-waṣalnā ilā al-qabri
sentences.l: And she did not cease giving-alms from the purse and saying: On behalf of the soul of ʿAzīza — until what (was) in the purse ran-out, and we arrived at the grave.
sentences.i: She went on giving from the purse, saying each time, “For the soul of ʿAzīza,” until the purse was empty and we had come to the grave.
sentences.n: lam tazal, “she did not cease”: with an imperfect, “she kept on”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَايَنَتِ الْقَبْرَ بَكَتْ وَرَمَتْ نَفْسَهَا عَلَيْهِ ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَخْرَجَتْ بِيكَارًا مِنَ الْفُولَاذِ وَمِطْرَقَةً لَطِيفَةً وَخَطَّتْ بِالْبِيكَارِ عَلَى الْحَجَرِ الَّذِي عَلَى رَأْسِ الْقَبْرِ خَطًّا لَطِيفًا وَرَسَمَتْ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿāyanati al-qabra bakat wa-ramat nafsahā ʿalayhi thumma innahā akhrajat bīkāran mina al-fūlādhi wa-miṭraqatan laṭīfatan wa-khaṭṭat bi-al-bīkāri ʿalā al-ḥajari alladhī ʿalā raʾsi al-qabri khaṭṭan laṭīfan wa-rasamat hādhihi al-abyāta taqūlu
sentences.l: And when she beheld the grave she wept and threw herself upon it. Then she brought out a compass of the steel, and a hammer, a fine (one), and traced with the compass upon the stone which (is) at the head of the grave a fine tracing, and inscribed these the verses, saying:
sentences.i: When she saw the grave she wept and threw herself on it. Then she took out a pair of steel compasses and a small hammer, and with the compasses she traced fine lines on the stone at the head of the grave, and inscribed these verses, saying:
sentences.n: bīkār, “pair of compasses”: a loan from Persian pargār; presumably its point marks out the letters and the hammer cuts them. bi-al-bīkāri, “with the compasses”: bi- of the instrument. The print puts a shadda on khaṭṭat, “she traced”.

sentences.t:
مَرَرْتُ بِقَبْرٍ دَارِسٍ وَسْطَ رَوْضَةٍ * عَلَيْهِ مِنَ النُّعْمَانِ سَبْعُ شَقَائِقِ
فَقُلْتُ لِمَنْ ذَا الْقَبْرُ جَاوَبَنِي الثَّرَى * تَادَّبْ فَهٰذَا الْقَبْرُ بَرْزَخُ عَاشِقِ
فَقُلْتُ رَعَاكَ اللّٰهُ يَامَيَّتَ الْهَوَى * وَاَسْكَنَكَ الْفِرْدَوْسَ اَعْلَى الشَّوَاهِقِ
مَسَاكِينُ اَهْلِ الْعِشْقِ حَتَّى قُبُورُهُمْ * عَلَيْهَا تُرَابُ الذُّلِّ بَيْنَ الْخَلَائِقِ
فَلَوْ اَسْتَطِعْ لَزَرَعْتُ حَوْلَكَ رَوْضَةً * وَاسْتَقَيْتُهَا مِنْ دَمْعِي الْمُنْدَافِقِ
sentences.tr:
marartu bi-qabrin dārisin wasṭa rawḍatin * ʿalayhi mina al-nuʿmāni sabʿu shaqāʾiqi
fa-qultu li-man dhā al-qabru jāwabanī al-tharā * taʾaddab fa-hādhā al-qabru barzakhu ʿāshiqi
fa-qultu raʿāka allāhu yā mayyita al-hawā * wa-askanaka al-firdawsa aʿlā al-shawāhiqi
masākīnu ahli al-ʿishqi ḥattā qubūruhum * ʿalayhā turābu al-dhulli bayna al-khalāʾiqi
fa-law astaṭiʿ la-zaraʿtu ḥawlaka rawḍatan * wa-istaqaytuhā min damʿī al-mundāfiqi
sentences.l:
I passed by a grave, effaced, in the midst of a garden; * upon it, of the anemone, seven blossoms.
And I said: Whose (is) this the grave? The soil answered me: * Be-mannerly! For this the grave (is) the barzakh of a lover.
And I said: May God watch-over you, O dead-one of the love, * and make you dwell (in) Paradise, highest of the heights.
Poor-ones of the people of the passion! Even their graves, * upon them (is) the dust of the abasement among the creatures.
And if I could, I would have planted around you a garden, * and watered it from my tear, the gushing.
sentences.i:
I passed a worn grave in the midst of a garden; * on it grew seven anemone flowers.
I asked, “Whose grave is this?” The earth replied: * “Mind your manners: this grave is a lover’s place of waiting.”
I said, “God keep you, you who died of love, * and give you a home in Paradise, highest of the heights!”
Pity the people of love: even on their graves * lies the dust of disgrace among mankind.
Had I the power, I would plant a garden round you, * and water it with my streaming tears.
sentences.n: The print points this verse, and it is copied as printed. al-nuʿmān: shaqāʾiq al-nuʿmān is the red anemone, the flower of graves and blood in poetry. barzakh, “barrier”: the place between death and the Resurrection where the dead wait. The print has تادّب without its hamza (taʾaddab, “mind your manners”), runs yā and mayyit together, and gives law astaṭiʿ, a jussive after law, which normally takes a perfect (law istaṭaʿtu); the poet treats law like in, “if”. la-zaraʿtu: la- opens the answer to law. The print points مَيَّت with a fatḥa on the yāʾ; the word is mayyit, “dead one”, and it is read mayyita here. al-mundāfiq is not a form the dictionaries give: it probably stands for al-mundafiq, “pouring out”, with a long ā, or for al-mutadāfiq, “gushing”, both from the same root, and is kept as printed and read so. ḥattā qubūruhum, “even their graves”: ḥattā here means “even”. marra bi-, “pass by”: the verb chooses the bi-. li-man, “whose”: li- of belonging.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَضَتْ وَهِيَ تَبْكِي وَمَضَيْتُ مَعَهَا إِلَى الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma maḍat wa-hiya tabkī wa-maḍaytu maʿahā ilā al-bustāni
sentences.l: Then she went-off, and she (was) weeping, and I went with her to the garden.
sentences.i: Then she went away weeping, and I went with her to the garden.
sentences.n: The print has دعها, a misprint for معها (maʿahā, “with her”), corrected here.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي بِاللَّهِ إِنَّكَ لَا تَنْقَطِعُ عَنِّي أَبَدًا فَقُلْتُ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī bi-allāhi innaka lā tanqaṭiʿu ʿannī abadan fa-qultu samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: And she said to me: By God, you (will) not cut-off from me, ever! And I said: Hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: She said to me, “By God, never stay away from me!” And I answered with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: bi-allāhi, “by God”: bi- of the oath. innaka lā tanqaṭiʿu, “you will not cut yourself off”: a plea put as a statement. inqaṭaʿa ʿan, “stay away from, stop visiting”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي وَاظَبْتُهَا وَأَتَرَدَّدُ عَلَيْهَا وَكُنْتُ كُلَّمَابِتُّ عِنْدَهَا تُحْسِنُ إِلَيَّ وَتُكْرِمُنِي وَتُسَائِلُنِي عَنِ الْكَلِمَتَيْنِ اللَّتَيْنِ قَالَتْهُمَا ابْنَةُ عَمِّي عَزِيزَةُ لِأُمِّي فَأُعِيدُهُمَا لَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innī wāẓabtuhā wa-ataraddadu ʿalayhā wa-kuntu kullamā bittu ʿindahā tuḥsinu ilayya wa-tukrimunī wa-tusāʾilunī ʿani al-kalimatayni allatayni qālathumā ibnatu ʿammī ʿAzīzatu li-ummī fa-uʿīduhumā lahā
sentences.l: Then I kept-constant (to) her and go-to-and-fro to her; and I was — whenever I spent-the-night with her, she does-good to me and honours me and asks me about the two words which the daughter of my uncle, ʿAzīza, said to my mother, and I repeat them to her.
sentences.i: After that I kept faithfully to her, coming and going to her house; and whenever I spent the night with her she treated me kindly and honoured me, and asked me about the two sayings my cousin ʿAzīza had spoken to my mother, and I would say them over to her.
sentences.n: The print has قاعيدهما, a misprint for فاعيدهما (fa-uʿīduhumā, “and I would repeat them”), corrected here. wāẓaba, “keep at, be constant in”: here with a direct object, “I kept to her”. taraddada ʿalā, “come and go to, visit often”. aḥsana ilā, “do good to”. li-ummī, “to my mother”: li- marks the one spoken to. sāʾala, “ask, question”: the print spells it تسائلني. The print runs كلما and بتّ together, with a shadda on the tāʾ (bittu, “I spent the night”), and marks the shadda of ilayya.

sentences.t: وَمَازِلْتُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْحَالِ مِنْ أَكْلٍ وَشُرْبٍ وَضَمٍّ وَعِنَاقٍ وَتَغْيِيرِ ثِيَابٍ مِنَ الْمَلَابِسِ الرِّقَاقِ حَتَّى غَلُظْتُ وَسَمِنْتُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ بِي هَمٌّ وَلَاحُزْنٌ وَنَسِيتُ بِنْتَ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: wa-mā ziltu ʿalā dhālika al-ḥāli min aklin wa-shurbin wa-ḍammin wa-ʿināqin wa-taghyīri thiyābin mina al-malābisi al-riqāqi ḥattā ghaluẓtu wa-samintu wa-lam yakun bī hammun wa-lā ḥuznun wa-nasītu binta ʿammī
sentences.l: And I did not cease (being) upon that the state, of eating and drinking and clasping and embracing and changing of clothes of the garments, the thin (ones), until I grew-thick and grew-fat; and there was not in me care and not grief, and I forgot the daughter of my uncle.
sentences.i: And so I went on, eating and drinking, clasping and embracing, and changing from one fine garment to another, until I grew stout and fat, with no care or grief in me; and I forgot my cousin.
sentences.n: dhālika al-ḥāl, “that state”: ḥāl may be either gender; feminine is the more usual, but the Nights often makes it masculine, as here. bī, “in me”: bi- marks where the care would be. The print runs وما and زلت, and ولا and حزن, together.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَزَلْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْحَالِ مُدَّةَ سَنَةٍ كَامِلَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal ʿalā dhālika al-ḥāli muddata sanatin kāmilatin
sentences.l: And I did not cease (being) upon that the state (for) a period of a year, complete.
sentences.i: I went on so for a whole year.

sentences.t: وَعِنْدَ رَاسِ السَّنَةِ دَخَلْتُ الْحَمَّامَ وَأَصْلَحْتُ شَانِي وَلَبِسْتُ بَدْلَةً فَاخِرَةً
sentences.tr: wa-ʿinda rāsi al-sanati dakhaltu al-ḥammāma wa-aṣlaḥtu shānī wa-labistu badlatan fākhiratan
sentences.l: And at the head of the year I entered the bath, and set-right my affair, and put on a suit, a splendid (one).
sentences.i: At the year’s end I went to the bath, put myself in order, and dressed in a splendid suit of clothes.
sentences.n: The print spells raʾs, “head”, and shaʾn, “affair”, without their hamza (راس, شاني); they are read rās and shān, as spoken. aṣlaḥa shaʾnahu, “set his affairs right”: here, made himself presentable. badla, “a suit of clothes”: a later word.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ شَرِبْتُ قَدَحَ شَرَابٍ وَشَمِمْتُ رَوَائِحَ قُمَاشِى الْمُضَمَّخِ بِأَنْوَاعِ الطِّيبِ وَأَنَا مُنْشَرِحُ الصَّدْرِ وَلَمْ أَعْلَمْ غَدْرَ الزَّمَانِ وَطَوَارِقَ الْحَدَثَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā kharajtu mina al-ḥammāmi sharibtu qadaḥa sharābin wa-shamimtu rawāʾiḥa qumāshī al-muḍammakhi bi-anwāʿi al-ṭībi wa-anā munshariḥu al-ṣadri wa-lam aʿlam ghadra al-zamāni wa-ṭawāriqa al-ḥadathāni
sentences.l: And when I came out from the bath, I drank a cup of wine, and smelled the scents of my stuff, the steeped with kinds of the perfume, and I (was) opened of the breast; and I did not know the treachery of the time and the night-knockers of the happenings.
sentences.i: When I came out of the bath I drank a cup of wine and breathed in the scent of my clothes, steeped in every kind of perfume; my heart was light, and I knew nothing of the treachery of Time and the blows that fall by night.
sentences.n: The print has الرمان (“the pomegranates”), a misprint for الزمان (al-zamān, “Time”), corrected here; ghadr al-zamān, “the treachery of Time”, is a set phrase, and al-zamān rhymes with al-ḥadathān. ṭawāriq, “night-knockers”: misfortunes that come knocking in the night. qumāsh, “stuff, cloth”: here his clothes, spelled with ى. bi-anwāʿ, “with kinds”: bi- of what it is steeped in. munshariḥ al-ṣadr, “open of breast”: light of heart. The print puts a shadda on al-muḍammakh, “steeped”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ وَقْتُ الْعِشَاءِ اشْتَاقَتْ نَفْسِي الذَّهَابَ إِلَيْهَا وَأَنَا سَكْرَانُ لَاأَدْرِي أَيْنَ أَتَوَجَّهُ فَذَهَبْتُ إِلَيْهَا فَمَالَ بِي السُّكْرُ إِلَى زُقَاقٍ يُقَالُ لَهُ زُقَاقُ النَّقِيبِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa waqtu al-ʿishāʾi ishtāqat nafsī al-dhahāba ilayhā wa-anā sakrānu lā adrī ayna atawajjahu fa-dhahabtu ilayhā fa-māla bī al-sukru ilā zuqāqin yuqālu lahu zuqāqu al-naqībi
sentences.l: And when the time of the evening came, my soul longed (for) the going to her; and I (was) drunk, not knowing where I head. And I went to her, and the drunkenness swerved with me to a lane (that) is said to it: the Lane of the Naqīb.
sentences.i: When the evening hour came I longed to go to her; and I was drunk, not knowing where I was heading. I set off for her house, and the drink turned me aside into a lane called the Lane of the Naqīb.
sentences.n: ishtāqat nafsī al-dhahāba, “my soul longed (for) going”: the print gives the object with no ilā, as spoken Arabic can. māla bihi, “carry him aside”: bi- makes the verb take him with it. al-naqīb, “the marshal”: an officer’s title, used for the head of a guild or a troop, and for the head of the Prophet’s descendants (naqīb al-ashrāf). yuqālu lahu, “it is called”: li- marks what is named. The print runs لا and ادري together, and puts a shadda on atawajjahu.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا أَنَا مَاشٍ فِي ذَلِكَ الزُّقَاقِ فَنَظَرْتُ بِعَيْنِي وَإِذَا أَنَا بِعَجُوزٍ مَاشِيَةٍ وَفِي إِحْدَى يَدَيْهَا شَمْعَةٌ مَوْقُودَةٌ وَفِي يَدِهَا الْأُخْرَى كِتَابٌ مَلْفُوفٌ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā anā māshin fī dhālika al-zuqāqi fa-naẓartu bi-ʿaynī wa-idhā anā bi-ʿajūzin māshiyatin wa-fī iḥdā yadayhā shamʿatun mawqūdatun wa-fī yadihā al-ukhrā kitābun malfūfun
sentences.l: And while I (was) walking in that the lane, then I looked with my eye, and behold, I (was) with an old-woman walking, and in one of her two hands a candle, lit, and in her hand, the other, a letter, rolled.
sentences.i: And as I was walking down that lane I looked, and there before me was an old woman walking along, with a lighted candle in one hand and a rolled-up letter in the other.
sentences.n: fa-naẓartu, “then I looked”: the fa- after baynamā is a spoken habit. bi-ʿaynī, “with my eye”: bi- of the instrument. wa-idhā anā bi-ʿajūzin, “and behold, an old woman”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. kitāb, here “a letter”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
